stops.name: Rome, birth in his father's household
stops.campa: Pedro León Maximiano María Subercaseaux Errázuriz is born in Rome on 10 December 1880, eldest son of the Chilean painter and future diplomat Ramón Subercaseaux Vicuña and of Amalia Errázuriz Urmeneta. The city that will one day hold his portrait of a pope receives him first as an infant in a household of easels and steamer trunks, his father sketching the Roman light between calls, his mother presiding over a family that will cross the Atlantic and the Alps a dozen times before he is grown. The canon opens its painter-saint the way it opens its warrior-saints: elsewhere, and already watched.

stops.name: Santiago, El Llano Subercaseaux, a happy house tried by grief
stops.campa: Between his father's postings the family returns to the ancestral chacra the Subercaseaux call El Llano, south of Santiago, whose name the barrio still carries. The first years are remembered as happy and united, the household drawn to the charm of doña Amalia, though sorrow visits too: two little daughters die young. Pedro and his brothers Luis and Juan run the grounds between European terms; Juan, the youngest, is already the more devout of the three, and will one day carry a Roman idea of monks home to Chile that his elder brother will help make walls and a choir.

stops.name: Douai, France, the English Benedictines' school
stops.campa: At eleven, Pedro and his brother Luis are enrolled by their parents in a school the exiled English Benedictine congregation runs at Douai in northern France, black-habited monks keeping an old rule in a foreign tongue for boys who are, themselves, foreigners to it. He does not know it yet, but the canon marks this as the first door of the cloister opening quietly before the boy who will spend his middle decades painting soldiers and his last painting saints: the school that will not let him go until, thirty years on, he asks to enter a house exactly like it.

stops.name: Berlin, the Royal Academy of Fine Arts
stops.campa: In 1896 the sixteen-year-old enters the Königliche Akademie der Künste under Anton von Werner, the Kaiser's own painter of battles, and studies under Julius Ehrentraut. Here the future painter of Chacabuco and Maipú learns the German discipline of the history canvas: the correct button on the correct uniform, the exact fall of a flag, the composition that reads as event and not as decoration. It is a craft made for empires and their founding myths alike; the boy from Santiago is absorbing, in Berlin, the very grammar he will later turn to Chile's own battles and cabildos.

stops.name: Rome, the studio of Lorenzo Vallés
stops.campa: The family's Roman years bring Pedro to the workshop of the Spanish painter Lorenzo Vallés, famous for his own vast history canvas of a mad queen keeping vigil over a coffin, and to the Scuola Libera del Nudo attached to Rome's Accademia. Between Raphael's frescoes and Vallés's theatrical royals, the young Chilean settles the argument Paris will soon put to him in the form of Cubism and Impressionism: he will paint as the Renaissance and the academy taught, bodies solid, light legible, history readable at a glance. Rome, the city of his birth, confirms rather than complicates his eye.

stops.name: Paris, the Académie Julian
stops.campa: In 1900 the family settles in Paris and Pedro joins the Académie Julian on the rue du Dragon, studying under Tony Robert-Fleury and Jules Joseph Lefebvre while, outside the studio windows, Impressionism has already won and Cubism is being born a few streets away. He watches both movements pass and finds them foreign to his own inclination; the record of his hand stays with Ingres and the neoclassicists even as the century turns against them. The canon reads this as fidelity, not backwardness: a painter keeping the one language in which a nation's glories can still be narrated plainly.

stops.name: Santiago, return with his father
stops.campa: In 1902 Pedro sails back to Chile with Ramón, twenty-one years old and carrying Berlin's discipline, Rome's classicism, and Paris's stubborn refusal of the new. He sets up a studio, an old wine bodega, by his own later account, where he works without pause, and looks at his adopted country with the eye of a man who has just spent six years learning exactly how to paint a nation's founding scenes. Two periods of Chilean history draw him above all others, he will write in his memoirs: the Conquest and the Independence, for what they hold of heroism and of the picturesque together.
stops.quote: Me atraían fuertemente dos épocas de nuestra historia: la Conquista y la Independencia, por lo que ellas representan de heroísmo y a la vez de pintoresco.

stops.name: Santiago, El Diario Ilustrado, the pseudonym P.S.
stops.campa: Under the initials P.S. the young painter begins illustrating for El Diario Ilustrado, drawing the colonial legends of Joaquín Díaz Garcés and the detective tales of Alberto Edwards for Pacífico Magazine. It is journeyman work, quick and daily, but it teaches him to read a scene for the single gesture that will carry a whole story to an illiterate glance, exactly the skill the coming battle canvases will need. Santiago's reading public meets, without quite knowing it, the hand that will one day fill the Salón de Honor of its own Congress with the discovery of the country itself.

stops.name: Quinta Normal, first medal of the Salón Oficial
stops.campa: At the Salón Oficial held in the Quinta Normal, Subercaseaux exhibits 'Primera Misa Celebrada en Chile' and an early 'Batalla de Maipú' and takes the first medal: official confirmation, four years out of the Paris academies, that the country has found its painter of national scenes. He will keep exhibiting here until 1912, gathering prizes in both historical and costumbrista categories, but this first medal is the hinge: the moment 'painter of Chile's glories' stops being an ambition and becomes, in the newspapers' own words, what he already is.

stops.name: Santiago, Von Pilsener is born in the pages of Zig-Zag
stops.campa: Under a second pseudonym, Lustig, 'cheerful' in the language of his Berlin years, Subercaseaux gives the weekly Zig-Zag a fat, tailcoated German professor named Baron Federico Von Pilsener, come to study Chile with a dachshund called Dudelsackpfeifergeselle trotting at his heel. Chile's first comic character runs seventeen irregular installments before folding in 1907, the whole joke turned inward: a European gaze exaggerated on purpose, so the country can laugh at its own manners through supposedly foreign eyes. One light stop in an otherwise grave itinerary, and the only place the future monk signs his work as a clown.
stops.quote: ...deseo de hacer resaltar, en forma humorística, nuestros propios defectos, exponiéndolos a la crítica de un imaginario observador europeo.
stops.quote_source: Pedro Subercaseaux, on his purpose in creating Von Pilsener, Memorias (1962)

stops.name: Santiago, marriage to Elvira Lyon Otaegui
stops.campa: Pedro marries Elvira Lyon Otaegui, a woman who shares his devotion to art, letters and religion in equal measure. The household they build over the next thirteen years is by every account a happy one; she poses, reads, and prays beside a husband who is fast becoming the most commissioned history painter in the Southern Cone. Neither yet knows how the marriage will end: not in estrangement but in a shared and deliberate vocation, dissolved by mutual consent and papal grace so that both might enter religion. The canon keeps this wedding day bright precisely because of what it will later cost them both to leave it well.

stops.name: Chacabuco, la Batalla de Chacabuco, the crossing made canvas
stops.campa: The Argentine government buys this canvas outright in 1908: San Martín on a white horse at the climax of the campaign, the cordillera he has just crossed still visible behind the smoke of the royalist collapse. Subercaseaux paints the general as the dispatch describes him: the twenty-four days, the highest mountains on earth passed, the tyrants ended, compressing the whole Army of the Andes into one arrested instant on the battlefield itself. The painter's stop lands exactly where San Martín's own itinerary in this atlas places its Chacabuco, and where O'Higgins's does too: three journeys converging on one hillside.
